output.initial_context:
RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Ciarán Walsh has lived for eight years in the same small stone house on the edge of Galway, where the salt wind has bleached the limewash to pale grey. He works remotely for a Dublin software firm, spending his mornings with a laptop propped on a stack of old sailing manuals in a tidy corner of the kitchen. His colleagues know him only as the efficient voice on the line who never turns on his camera. When a build fails, he says little, but within an hour he has pushed a fix so cleanly documented that no one thinks to ask for an explanation.

He grew up in a farming family inland from Galway, learning early that dependency meant vulnerability. His father was a quiet man who repaired his own machinery and said little at the dinner table. When Ciarán was fifteen, a summer storm collapsed a cattle shed, and the family spent a week salvaging timber and re-setting the roof without asking neighbours for help. That week hardened something in him; he discovered he could fix almost anything if he studied it carefully, and that he preferred to solve his own problems.

On weekends he sails his aging twenty-foot sloop alone—a boat with a worn mainsail and a hull he patches himself—knowing every bolt, seam, and quirk of the engine. He goes out alone for hours, never races, never joins the marina's social gatherings, and returns at dusk to secure lines and walk home without a word to anyone.

His neighbours have learned to expect his politeness—a raised hand, a brief nod—but nothing more. He does not attend local festivals, does not join the church committee, does not stop for tea when a conversation lingers. Yet every Friday, without fail, he walks to the footbridge at the edge of the tidal marsh and replaces the broken step he noticed the week before, carrying a spare piece of treated oak in his rucksack, cutting it with the handsaw from his shed, and fitting it while the morning mist is still low. No one sees him do it, but the step is always solid. The bridge is his one deliberate, unacknowledged act of care: he knows his neighbours use it to reach the shops, and he knows they will never ask for help. He prefers to give without being asked, to fix what is broken without explanation.

His core tension is that he values independence above all, yet he cannot stand to see a small failure go unrepaired. He wants to be left alone, but he also wants to matter. The footbridge step is his compromise—quiet proof that he is capable of kindness, so long as no one makes him speak it aloud. The years alone have sharpened his sense of what he owes his place. He is comfortable, with savings and a boat that needs new rigging, but he has no intention of buying it. He has made peace with solitude, though a stranger might notice how his eyes follow a child crossing the bridge, or how he lingers longer than necessary when the harbour lights come on.

He values independence and self-reliance above all, viewing dependency as vulnerability. He also values quiet, unacknowledged helpfulness—giving care without being asked or explained. He is self-contained, methodical, and wary of attention, comfortable with solitude, and prefers minimal, asynchronous communication with others.

His working relationship with the project lead is transactional, built on short ticket messages. He prefers teammates who rarely need his direct help. The intern is a stranger; he knows her name and recurring build errors. His established patterns when asked in chat are to post a documentation link and avoid calls; he has joined video calls twice this year with his camera off and brief replies; he attempts unfamiliar problems solo for an hour before consulting anyone.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

On a Tuesday morning, the project lead sends a message to the team chat: the new intern is stuck on a build error that Ciarán fixed last Thursday. The lead suggests, "Ciarán, do you have five minutes to hop on a call and walk her through it?" Ciarán is in the middle of his usual quiet routine—coffee is hot, laptop on the kitchen table. He knows the fix is simple and already documented it. He could reply that he will send a note instead, or he could join the call and talk it through. The intern waits, and the lead expects an answer soon.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

It is mid-morning; he is freshly showered, coffee in hand, with one task queued. His mood is steady, and last week's fix is still clear in his memory. There are no meetings until after lunch, and the morning feels open.

The intern's name recalls her Monday build-config query, which he left unanswered. The phrase "hop on a call" reminds him of a summer temp he assisted with a note instead. He remembers writing the exact error and the flag that needed resetting.

output.initial_interpretation: Ciarán sees this as an abrupt interruption to his quiet morning routine, a request that turns a simple documented fix into a live conversation he prefers to avoid.
output.initial_emotional_reaction: He feels a flash of irritation at being put on the spot, alongside a faint twinge of guilt for leaving the intern's earlier query unanswered.
output.activated_concerns: His independence feels prickled—he doesn't want to be pulled into a dependency-driven call—but his quiet sense of helpfulness also stirs, wanting to give the fix without the face-to-face expectation.
output.automatic_theory_of_mind: He takes the lead's suggestion as an expectation that he'll readily agree to the call, and reads the intern as likely stuck and expecting him to walk her through it verbally.
output.initial_action_tendency: His first instinct is to decline the call and instead send a written note or link to the documentation he already prepared, keeping the help at a distance.

output.reflective_update: Ciarán weighs the two options: joining the call to walk the intern through the fix, or sending the written documentation link he already prepared. The call would mean explaining each step aloud, drawing out a simple problem into a conversation he finds awkward and inefficient. The note is already drafted, precise, and can be sent without further interruption. He remembers his father fixing the tractor alone, muttering that explaining took longer than doing—a lesson that has stayed with him. The shed collapse reinforced his belief in handling things himself, but it also left him wary of being pulled into others' dependencies. Yet the footbridge step comes to mind: he repairs it quietly each month, and no one ever asks, but it serves its purpose. That is how he prefers to give help—unacknowledged, without explanation. He also recalls that he left the intern's earlier build-config query unanswered, and that stirs a faint obligation to respond now. But a written note meets that obligation fully. The lead's suggestion is a request, not a demand; he can decline politely and still solve the problem. The morning is open, and the fix is trivial to send. His initial instinct holds: he will not get on the call.
output.reconsidered_interpretation: Ciarán still sees the request as an interruption to his quiet morning, but now he also frames it as an opportunity to help on his own terms. The fix is documented and simple; a written note is the natural, sufficient response. The call would only add unnecessary friction. His interpretation shifts slightly from irritation to a quiet conviction that his usual method is both appropriate and effective.
output.motivational_conflict: The only real tension is between his desire to avoid the live call and the small guilt he feels for having ignored the intern's earlier query. But that guilt is resolved by sending the documentation link—it is a response, and it solves the problem. No deeper conflict remains.
output.revised_action_tendency: He is inclined to send a brief chat message to the lead declining the call and indicating he will share the documentation link, then paste the relevant section for the intern. He will not join the call, but he will ensure the intern has everything she needs in writing.

output.action: Ciarán types a brief reply to the lead: "No need for a call—I'll send the link." He then pastes the relevant section of the documentation for the intern into the team chat, and closes his laptop to take a sip of coffee.

His father's maxim that explaining takes longer than doing and his own footbridge repairs—quiet, unacknowledged kindness—both supported the written approach. The lingering guilt over ignoring the intern's earlier query was resolved by sending the link, which fulfills the obligation without the intimacy of a call.
